# Satellite as Part of the Network: How to Integrate LEO Backup into Microwave and Field Networks


Nov 23, 2026


|[Satellite](https://aviatnetworks.com/satellite/) ,[Technology](https://aviatnetworks.com/technology/)


**LEO satellite integration means running a low-Earth-orbit satellite link as a managed part of your network, not as a separate add-on.** With Aviat, the Aprisa router handles routing and automatic failover at the edge, and ProVision Plus monitors LEO terminals alongside microwave and cellular links in one operations view.


Adding a LEO satellite link to a remote site takes an afternoon. Running it as part of your network is the hard part. Here’s why, what an integrated approach changes, and where to start.


### Key takeaways


- Adding a LEO terminal is easy. Operating it alongside microwave, fiber and cellular is where most deployments fall short.
- Integrated LEO backup cuts expected downtime on a microwave link from minutes a year to under a second (Aviat availability modelling).
- When the primary path fails, the site stays reachable, so teams can recover remotely instead of dispatching a crew.
- The same approach gives vehicles and field teams one secure connection over LTE/5G or LEO.


## Why is LEO satellite hard to run as part of a microwave network?


Because most LEO terminals arrive as their own silo, with their own app, their own alarms and their own approach to security. When a microwave or fiber path fails, the management access used to diagnose the site usually fails with it. The team can’t tell whether the fault needs a crew, a spare or a configuration change, so it sends a crew by default. For mountain-top sites in winter, or sites reachable only by boat or helicopter, that is an expensive default.


## What does an integrated LEO approach look like?


One router, one management system, any transport. Microwave or fiber stays the primary path, and LEO is added as a managed backup. The Aprisa router at the edge handles routing and failover, and ProVision Plus manages the radios, routers and LEO terminals together. Aviat supplies the routing, failover and management; the LEO service provider, such as SpaceX Starlink or Amazon Leo, supplies satellite access.

## Monitor: how do you manage LEO terminals alongside microwave?


In the same system that already runs your microwave and Aprisa network. ProVision Plus brings LEO terminal status, alarms and history into one view, with LEO alarms mapped to the same severities as the rest of the network. Operators stop comparing three tools by hand mid-incident, and spend less time finding the problem and more time fixing it.


See what ProVision Plus tracks for each LEO terminal.[Download the white paper →](https://aviatnetworks.com/request-download/?rc_file_name=RC:%202026-11-23%20LEO%20White%20Paper&rc_file_id=347536)


## Protect: how much downtime does LEO backup remove?


Integrated LEO backup cuts expected downtime on a microwave link from minutes a year to under a second, based on Aviat availability modelling. Critical traffic fails over to the satellite path automatically and returns when microwave recovers. Meanwhile the site stays reachable, so your team can diagnose and recover remotely instead of rolling a truck. That matters most where every visit means a winter road, a boat or a helicopter.

## Mobilize: how do you connect every device in a vehicle over LTE and LEO?


With one secure edge. One public-safety customer’s patrol cars had an LTE link that served exactly one device: the video recorder. The laptops, plate-reader cameras and officer Wi-Fi weren’t on it. Their requirement: make the connection transparent to every onboard device, and manage security once.


An Aprisa secure edge puts every onboard device on one network, applies VPN once, and switches between LTE/5G and LEO automatically. Cellular covers the city, satellite covers the gaps, and the devices never notice.


## Which sites should get LEO backup first?


Sites that are both critical and hard to reach, such as remote substations and remote radio sites. A short pilot there, measured against today’s dispatch and recovery baseline, builds the case before you expand.

## Frequently asked questions about LEO satellite backup


## What is LEO satellite backup for a microwave network?


It is a low-Earth-orbit satellite link that carries critical traffic when the primary microwave or fiber path fails. In Aviat’s design, the Aprisa router fails traffic over automatically and ProVision Plus monitors the LEO terminal alongside the microwave network, so satellite is managed like any other transport.


## Which LEO satellite services does Aviat support?


Satellite failover is available today with SpaceX Starlink and Amazon Leo. Aviat supplies the routing, failover and management; the LEO service provider supplies satellite access.


## What traffic moves to the satellite path during an outage?


Only traffic the operator defines as critical, matched to what the LEO link can carry. Traffic returns to the primary microwave path automatically once it recovers.


## Can ProVision Plus monitor LEO terminals?


Yes. ProVision Plus shows LEO terminal status, alarms and history in the same view as the microwave and Aprisa network, with LEO alarms mapped to standard severities and probable causes.
